pr_body:
This adds new query that allows searching for vectors within a similarity boundary that match a query vector.

This only works against `dense_vector` fields where `index: true`. 

`num_candidates` is still required as this controls the nearest-neighbor vector search accuracy. For each shard the query will search `num_candidates` and only keep those that are within the provided `similarity` boundary.

For example, when using the `l2_norm` indexed similarity value, this could be considered a `radius` query.

This query can be used as any other normal query and can be combined with other queries with a `bool` query.

Additionally, this query can be used within a `filter` context, but note underlying implementation will still need to compare vector distances and scores to apply the provided similarity threshold limitation.

closes: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/84929
pr_comments: Hi @benwtrent, I've created a changelog YAML for you.
Hi @benwtrent, I've updated the changelog YAML for you. *Note* that since this PR is labelled `release highlight`, you need to update the changelog YAML to fill out the extended information sections.

There was some back and forth between @benwtrent , @jpountz and myself around what the best way to expose the vector similarity is. We decided to go for a simpler alternative to start with, which consists of adding a similarity parameter to the existing knn section (see #94828). We'd like to get feedback on that solution and its limitations from users, and possibly evaluate at a later time adding vector query capabilities to the query DSL like this PR was attempting to do, in which case we said we would consider adding knn query support to the query DSL, and not only the similarity bit.

issue_context.title: Maximum radius for kNN search API
issue_context.body:
### Description

The API for approximate kNN search with `dense_vector` is 🔥.
One of my current use cases involves a maximum distance check, as in the [fixed-radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-radius_near_neighbors) variant of nearest neighbors.

It would be a nice addition to the API in my opinion to have the ability to add a radius filter to results. It may even provide opportunities to bail early when performing the HNSW search, but that could be tricky since sometimes the first approximate neighbor is actually farther away from the second approximate neighbor.

In addition to that, there are some other advantages by adding the maximum distance to the API and implementing it server side: when results from shards are aggregated to find the combined ANN across the index.

(I apologize if this comes across as overly prescriptive or if I made incorrect assumptions. I'm fairly certain that this can decently achieved client-side with some simple filtering and by increasing `num_candidates`)
comments:
@rw-access thanks for the feedback! I have also wondered if it'd be helpful to expose a "radius limit" capability. I agree it's more natural to implement it within Elasticsearch rather than client side.

Could you give a little more context on your use case? This can help us as we think through the API (for example is it a radius limit on the kNN search, or should there be a separate "radius query" that matches every document within the radius)?

Thanks for the reply @jtibshirani!

My use case is twofold: DBSCAN and near-duplicate detection.

For DBSCAN, I know my radius already (experimentally derived) and want to build clusters given that. This means that there are a lot of calls I make where I want to collect all the neighbors within a specific radius (with my current iterative approach I actually only need to collect the 1-2 closest within the radius).

For my usage it's perfectly okay for this to be approximate and that's an acceptable tradeoff. Also, when clustering with DBSCAN using approximate kNN, if point A doesn't find neighbor B within the approximate search + radius filter, there's a decent chance that B finds A.

For near-duplicate detection, I'm essentially doing a quick lookup with the parameters: k=1, num_candidates=10 and then do a client side check for the maximum radius.

Whether that's the same API or not is a good question. I'm not sure how HNSW handles exact kNN within a radius and if that as performant. For me at least, I don't need to be as exact. I would defer to your expertise.
Are there any updates on this issue? We would find a lot of use in this feature

@jtibshirani hi! 

We want to combine symbolic and semantic searches together and we would greatly benefit from this feature, as it would allow us to filter out irrelevant documents found through semantics (ANN). I understand that you're not working for ElasticSearch anymore, but perhaps you could forward it to right people.
In our case, our vectors are L2-normalized and we would rather use the dot product (i.e. cosine similarity) threshold, but we'll be fine with L2 distance, too.

> In our case, our vectors are L2-normalized and we would rather use the dot product (i.e. cosine similarity) threshold, but we'll be fine with L2 distance, too.

thanks @anordertoreclaim , I have been thinking more on this, and I think it will be possible to simply utilize whatever distance metric was used to build the index (e.g. configured in the vector field). 

I will get working on this this week.

I called it `vector_similarity` as it seemed to me the only "radius" would be if we did `l2_norm`. 

But, effectively, it takes a similarity threshold that vectors must be "this similar" to be considered. 

In the `l2_norm` case, `similarity` can be considered the radius of the sphere of dimension `dims`.

At each shard, it will gather `num_candidates`, only keeping docs where the vectors are within the similarity threshold. The document `_score` is the same as KNN and it supports `boost`.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/93574

@anordertoreclaim @rw-access @nariman9119
@anordertoreclaim @rw-access @nariman9119 ^ Have you tried the new `similarity` field in `knn`?
Closing this issue. If the current similarity_threshold logic is inadequate, we can reopen or add new functionality.

review_comments:
I wonder if you could do some random invariant test as well, e.g. that for random query and docs you never return docs whose distance is greater than specified query radius. And similarly for the other metrics.

For this one, I would do something like generate uniform data over say hypercube of side length L and query uniformly in same hypercube and chose a query `radius = f * (dim)^(1/2) * L` for say `f < 0.25`, i.e. at least less quarter the diagonal so you have a good chance of included and excluded points. Probably also not setting `dim` too high or you get weird concentration of measure effects.
Dividing by `1 << 15` may well be correct but seems surprising to me. I would expect this to be `1 << 8`, i.e. `= 2 * 1 << 7`.
@tveasey this is from Lucene to capture the score transformation.
This seems weird to me. Scores will all end up very small. But for definite we need to match Lucene here. Perhaps this is something to revisit in Lucene.

I think I got confused because I thought that `num_candidates` in the `knn` query was to control the visited limit of the Lucene's LeafReader:
```
public abstract TopDocs searchNearestVectors(
      String field, byte[] target, int k, Bits acceptDocs, int visitedLimit) throws IOException;
```
But in fact this visitedLimited is controlled by the cost of the filter in our implementation so `num_candidate` in knn query really means how many candidates we return per shard to compute the global top k.
I am failing to understand why though. If the `knn` query returns 10k docs per shard and then it is reduced by the coordinator to a top k, why would returning more than topk docs per shard helps? I am sure I am missing something obvious so sorry in advance for the noob question.

~~Ok I think I got it now, for knn the num_candidates is to allow more post filtering locally on the shard and what is sent back to the coordinating node is the final shard topK after applying the post filter. This global topK is really a pain to understand correctly for me but that's maybe just because I am slow ;).~~

`num_candidates` is the equivalent of `efSearch` in the other implementations for HNSW. The number of candidates that we keep in the queue to compute the final topK. Sorry for the noise. If that's the case then I don't see why there should be a difference between the `knn` query and this new `vector_similarity`. They are identical.

I am concerned by the duplication with the `KnnVectorQueryBuilder`. The similarity threshold is a feature of any knn query so I don't see why we need to separate here. I understand that the `knn` section has different semantics regarding the aggregations and maybe alias filters but that shouldn't prevent using the same query internally.
Could we expose the `knn` query in the query section instead? If we're adding a way to do knn in the query section (as opposed to the knn section) that should be fine to reuse. The fact that aggregations would behave differently is tied to where the query appears, not what type of query I am running.

This seems like the crux. I'm assuming Lucene converts to [0,1] scores for Euclidean by `1 / (1 + ||q - d||)`, cosine by `(1 + q^t d) / 2`, and then everything makes sense. (For dot it also uses `(1 + q^t d) / 2`? This wouldn't then be [0,1] or indeed always positive, or is this the issue with dot only supporting unit vectors at present?)

As an aside, I was sort of expecting these operations to be encapsulated by some Lucene class, so you don't rely on this matching how the knn query scores.

> As an aside, I was sort of expecting these operations to be encapsulated by some Lucene class, so you don't rely on this matching how the knn query scores.

It will be eventually.

Right now Lucene simply gives us score information from two vectors. It does not have mechanisms to transform the similarity to the final document score.

Why not reusing `org.elasticsearch.common.lucene.search.function.MinScoreScorer` ? It should be straightforward to add the support for boost there. The nice thing about the existing `MinScoreScorer` is that it exposes a twoPhaseIterator that should speed up queries with another restrictive filter.
